titre: The Horned Viking Helmet, a 19th-Century Image
accroche: No horned Viking helmet has ever been found. The horned helmets of Viksø, in Denmark, date from the Bronze Age.
contenu_vulgarise:
The Viking of the movies wears a metal helmet topped with two horns. Yet no helmet of that shape has ever been found at a Viking Age site, and the nearly complete helmet we know is round, made of iron, and has none.

## What the digs have yielded

In 1943, while clearing a field near the Gjermundbu farm, at Haugsbygd, in Buskerud county in Norway, a very rich male grave of the 10th century is uncovered. The helmet it contained has been restored from nine fragments: it is round, made of iron, formed of four plates. According to Science Norway, what looks like a kind of pair of spectacles protects the face. For the World-Tree Project, it is the only Viking Age helmet found in Scandinavia; Wikipedia counts five known, fragments included, of which only two can be reconstructed.

Ingrid Ystgaard, cited by Science Norway, confirms it: no helmet from the Viking period with horns has ever been found. According to Wikipedia, the texts of the time regularly mention helmets without ever mentioning a horned headdress. If such a headdress existed during the Viking Age, historians believe it was not worn regularly.

## Horned helmets do exist, but earlier

Two horned helmets were found in 1942 in a peat bog on the island of Zealand, at Viksø, in Denmark. They date from the Bronze Age: about 2,000 years before the Vikings according to Science Norway, while the radiocarbon dating reported by Wikipedia (which spells it Veksø) places the latest deposit between 907 and 857 BCE. They were probably used in religious ceremonies, before being deposited in the bog as an offering. Science Norway also cites horned helmets from the Merovingian period (around 550-800), which Ystgaard does not consider war helmets.

## Where the image comes from

The first complete cycle of Wagner's Ring tetralogy opens the first Bayreuth festival in August 1876, from the 13th to the 17th. Wagner commissioned Carl Emil Doepler to design the costumes, and the World-Tree project at University College Cork writes that Doepler chose to adorn the helmets with horns. The same project adds that before that date, the Vikings' helmets were depicted with wings, while horned helmets were reserved for barbarians, citing Roberta Frank (2000).

The sources do not agree on the very first example, however. Michael Echter, a German painter close to Wagner, decorated the palace of Ludwig II of Bavaria with murals inspired by the Ring, and Scandinavian Archaeology sees in them one of the first examples of horned helmets associated with Norse mythology, without dating these paintings. The Danish painter Lorens Frølich, placed by the same page among the creators of the image, signs a painting in 1877. According to Wikipedia, the idea was also spread in part by enthusiasts of the Götiska Förbundet, a society founded in Stockholm in 1811. As to where these artists found their inspiration, Scandinavian Archaeology writes that it is unknown.

repere.texte: The Gjermundbu helmet (Norway, discovered in 1943) is one of only two Viking Age helmets that could be reconstructed: round, made of iron, formed of four plates, restored from nine fragments. It has no horns.

carte.punch: No horned Viking helmet has been found. The horned helmets of Viksø are far older.
carte.idee: The Gjermundbu helmet, found in Norway in 1943, is round, made of iron, with no horns. The two horned helmets of Viksø (Denmark) date from the Bronze Age, well before the Vikings. The image of horned Vikings is a 19th-century association, popularized by Wagner's costumes in 1876.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The complete tetralogy cycle opens the first Bayreuth festival in 1876, August 13-17.

quiz.question: Where does the image of the Viking with a horned helmet come from?
choix: It appears in the 19th century, notably with the costumes of Wagner's Ring tetralogy in 1876
It comes from the medieval sagas, which describe Viking chiefs wearing horned helmets
It reproduces the helmets from the Gjermundbu grave, found in Norway in 1943 and adorned with two horns
It continues a Bronze Age practice that remained common among the Viking warriors themselves
quiz.explication: The sources place the association in the 19th century, with the Bayreuth costumes in 1876. The Gjermundbu helmet has no horns, the texts of the period cite helmets without ever mentioning horns, and the horned helmets of Viksø date from the Bronze Age, well before the Vikings.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when were the two horned helmets of Viksø discovered?
choix: In 1942, in a peat bog on the island of Zealand, in Denmark
In 1943, in a field near Gjermundbu, in Norway
In the 19th century, during railway construction in Sweden
In 1876, during digs organized for the Bayreuth festival
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The two Viksø helmets were found in 1942 in a peat bog on the island of Zealand. The date of 1943 and the Gjermundbu location concern another helmet, Norwegian and hornless; the other two options are invented.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who chose to adorn with horns the helmets in the costumes for Wagner's Ring tetralogy, at Bayreuth in 1876?
choix: Richard Wagner himself, for the first Bayreuth festival
King Ludwig II of Bavaria, the composer's patron
Carl Emil Doepler, commissioned by Wagner to design the costumes
The Danish painter Lorens Frølich, author of an 1877 painting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the World-Tree Project, Wagner commissioned Carl Emil Doepler to design the costumes, and it was Doepler who chose to adorn the helmets with horns. Wagner himself, Ludwig II, and Frølich play other roles in the story of this image, not this one.
